title: The Noise-Transmission Burden of Diffusion Network: Why Image Prediction Can Outperform Noise Prediction

paper.title: The Noise-Transmission Burden of Diffusion Network: Why Image Prediction Can Outperform Noise Prediction
paper.abstract:
Abstract Clean-image prediction ( x x -prediction) and noise prediction yield equivalent population-optimal denoisers, yet can perform very differently in finite diffusion networks.
For noisy input Y t Y_{t} with noise standard deviation σ t \sigma_{t} , a noise predictor f ε , t f_{\varepsilon,t} induces the clean-image estimate X ^ 1 = Y t − σ t ​ f ε , t ​ ( Y t ) \widehat{X}_{1}=Y_{t}-\sigma_{t}f_{\varepsilon,t}(Y_{t}) .
This reveals a noise-transmission burden : the predictor must preserve information needed to cancel the input corruption.
Under Gaussian corruption of d d -dimensional data, a linear input bottleneck of rank r < d r<d imposes a denoising-error floor σ t 2 ​ ( d − r ) \sigma_{t}^{2}(d-r) even with unrestricted downstream computation, while the corresponding optimal risk for image prediction remains bounded.
EDM attenuates this bottleneck contribution at high noise; exact preconditioning cancels it at every noise level.
Without an input bottleneck, assuming exact affine recovery of the noisy patch from the model representation, we characterize how the covariance spectrum of corrections beyond linear denoising determines the width required above the patch dimension.
ImageNet experiments with JiT show that measured denoising losses reflect the predicted bottleneck floor and its attenuation or cancellation through preconditioning.
Further widening yields larger relative denoising gains at low noise, where corrections beyond linear denoising spread across more directions, consistent with our spectral characterization of the required model width.
Together, these results provide a denoising-based account of practical generation-quality gaps across prediction targets, preconditioning choices, and model widths.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Why should predicting the clean image be easier than predicting the noise added to it? At the population optimum, image, noise, and velocity predictors are related by simple identities and yield the same denoiser. Yet their performance can differ substantially in finite networks. JiT demonstrates this gap in pixel-space diffusion Transformers: image prediction succeeds with coarse patches and narrow input embeddings in settings where noise or velocity prediction performs poorly ( Li and He, 2025 ) . Understanding this mismatch matters for choosing prediction targets and allocating model capacity. It raises a concrete architectural question: what information must each predictor retain from its input for accurate denoising, and can it preserve that information when an input bottleneck reduces the representation dimension below the patch dimension? Prior work shows that both data geometry and architecture influence prediction-target preference ( Li and He, 2025 ; Jin and Wang, 2026 ; Gagneux et al., 2026 ) , but does not quantify how architectural constraints on retained input information affect denoising. Existing output-rank bounds establish a loss floor when predictions are confined to a restricted output subspace ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) . A complementary limitation arises when the architecture discards noisy-input information: even an unrestricted decoder may then lack the information needed for accurate denoising. How does this error depend on the input bottleneck and noise level, even with unrestricted downstream computation, and how does an explicit input path change it? Once input compression is removed, how much additional width is needed to retain the noisy input while representing corrections beyond linear denoising? Appendix C reviews existing results and their relation to these questions. We address these questions through the clean-image estimate induced by a noise predictor. For a clean image X 1 ∈ ℝ d X_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and normalized Gaussian-corrupted observation Y t = X 1 + σ t ​ ε Y_{t}=X_{1}+\sigma_{t}\varepsilon , the estimate is X ^ 1 = Y t − σ t ​ f ε , t ​ ( Y t ) \widehat{X}_{1}=Y_{t}-\sigma_{t}f_{\varepsilon,t}(Y_{t}) . The explicit input term carries the corruption, and the learned branch must supply the noise contribution needed to cancel it. We call the requirement to retain this information a noise-transmission burden . This viewpoint connects input compression, output preconditioning, and hidden width through their effects on attainable denoising accuracy. Based on this viewpoint, our theoretical analysis and ImageNet experiments with JiT yield three linked results. 1. An input bottleneck imposes a denoising-error floor for noise prediction that grows quadratically with noise. Theorem 1 and Corollary 2 establish the floor σ t 2 ​ ( d − r ) \sigma_{t}^{2}(d-r) when the architecture imposes a linear input bottleneck of rank r < d r<d , even with unrestricted downstream computation. The result requires only a finite second moment for the clean data and no manifold assumption; the corresponding optimal risk for image prediction remains bounded under the same bottleneck. Experiments show denoising loss approaching the floor at high noise (Figure 2 b), with affine noise-recovery probes below the ceiling (Figure 3 ; Table 3 ). 2. EDM alleviates the noise-transmission burden at high noise; exact preconditioning cancels it. Theorem 3 and Corollary 4 characterize how an explicit input path changes the denoising-error floor imposed by the input bottleneck. EDM suppresses it at high noise, while exact preconditioning removes it at every noise level. Consistent with this analysis, EDM improves FID from 412.11 412.11 for noise prediction to 52.28 52.28 , and exact preconditioning reaches 9.15 9.15 , close to image prediction’s 9.13 9.13 (Figure 2 a). Concurrently, EDM’s denoising loss approaches that of image prediction at high noise, exact preconditioning tracks image prediction across noise levels (Figures 2 b and 7 ), and learned skip coefficients closely track their exact-preconditioning values at moderate and high noise (Figure 6 a). 3. Without an input bottleneck, corrections beyond linear denoising determine how far model width must exceed the patch dimension. Assuming the noisy input patch can be recovered exactly by an affine readout of the model representation, Theorem 5 and Corollary 6 characterize the minimum representation width needed for a chosen level of denoising accuracy. Since such a representation already supports linear denoising, the additional width needed depends on the remaining nonlinear correction. Both the correction’s magnitude and the distribution of its variance across directions matter. In our experiments, modest widening improves generation, denoising, and affine noisy-input recovery (Figures 4 a–b, 5 , and 9 ). Further widening yields larger relative denoising gains at low noise, where the required nonlinear corrections are spread across more directions than at high noise (Figures 4 b–c and 8 b–c).

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: We test our theoretical predictions with experiments on ImageNet. Sections 3.1 and 3.2 show that an input bottleneck, arising when model width d h d_{h} is smaller than patch dimension d p d_{p} or the input passes through a narrow patch embedding, limits noise recovery (Theorem 1 ) and imposes a denoising-error floor (Corollary 2 ). EDM-style preconditioning alleviates this discarded-noise contribution at high noise, while exact preconditioning eliminates it (Theorem 3 and Corollary 4 ). To test these predictions, we use JiT-B/16 ( Li and He, 2025 ) on ImageNet256 with a 768 → 128 → 768 768\to 128\to 768 bottleneck patch embedding, comparing prediction targets and output preconditioning through FID-10K, fixed-time denoising loss, and noise-recovery probes. Section 3.3 shows that when d h ≥ d p d_{h}\geq d_{p} , the additional model width needed to approximate the population-optimal denoiser is determined by the covariance spectrum of its residual beyond the best affine denoiser, under Assumption 1 (Theorem 5 and Corollary 6 ). This residual describes the correction beyond linear denoising needed at each time t t . To examine this width requirement, we remove the bottleneck embedding and widen noise predictors from d h = d p d_{h}=d_{p} to 2 ​ d p 2d_{p} , using ImageNet256 with d p = 768 d_{p}=768 and ImageNet128 with d p = 192 d_{p}=192 . We also probe affine recovery of the noisy input from the hidden representation to assess empirical support for Assumption 1 . Finally, we use a pretrained ADM denoiser ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ) as a proxy for the population-optimal denoiser to estimate the residual spectrum directly. Both suites use X t = t ​ X 1 + ( 1 − t ) ​ ε X_{t}=tX_{1}+(1-t)\varepsilon , so σ t = ( 1 − t ) / t \sigma_{t}=(1-t)/t and small t t means high noise. Denoising, probe, and residual-spectrum measurements use the ImageNet validation split, held out from backbone training. Experimental details and additional results are provided in Appendix B .

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: Our analysis has several limitations. Our width characterization relies on Assumption 1 : the noisy patch must be exactly recoverable through an affine readout of the representation. This describes one representation strategy rather than a necessary property of all successful noise predictors. Within our unrestricted representation class, width 2 ​ d p 2d_{p} already suffices to represent the population-optimal denoiser. Further improvements in generation from widening beyond 2 ​ d p 2d_{p} are not characterized by our current denoising-risk theory; explaining these gains is left for future work. Moreover, although our experiments use networks shared across noise levels and evaluate both denoising and generation, the theoretical analysis treats each noise level separately, leaving open how parameter sharing changes the attainable tradeoffs. It also characterizes denoising accuracy without establishing how errors propagate through sampling or translate into differences between generated and target distributions.

sections.heading: Appendix C Related literature
sections.text: Prediction targets and data geometry. JiT motivates image prediction through the manifold hypothesis and demonstrates its advantage in coarse-patch Transformers, including models with narrow input embeddings ( Li and He, 2025 ) . Jin and Wang (2026) connect data geometry to the preferred mixture of clean data and noise in the prediction target through an analysis of a linear predictor shared across time, and propose k k -Diff to learn this mixture jointly with the network. These works establish the importance of data geometry when choosing a prediction target. A further question is whether the architecture preserves the input information needed to predict that target accurately. Even directions containing little clean-image information can carry noise that must be canceled when forming a clean-image estimate from a noise predictor.
